content: 1. Health education facilities and programs should be designed to be socially accountable and sustainable, ensuring they meet the needs of the communities they serve. 2. Investments in rural infrastructure development should be linked to health education initiatives, aligning with broader sustainable development goals. 3. When implementing policies to locate health worker training programs closer to rural and remote areas, it is essential to consider the specific context and setting of these regions. 4. Various approaches can be adopted, such as establishing rural health training schools, creating rural campuses for urban-based institutions (e.g., Northern Ontario School of Medicine), or developing rurally based training programs like the Wisconsin Nurse Residency Program. These efforts can be supported by fostering collaborations between communities and training institutions. 5. Ethiopia provides an example of accelerating health worker production by converting 20 non-teaching hospitals into training centers through partnerships with nearby universities. 6. Community engagement and support from local stakeholders are critical for the long-term success of such interventions. 7. Involving local communities in the development of multidisciplinary rural health worker education facilities and programs ensures social accountability and relevance to local needs. 8. Decisions regarding the location and infrastructure of these facilities should consider the benefits, impacts, and equity outcomes for rural communities. 9. Deep community involvement can lead to cost-effective and feasible plans, as demonstrated by the Zamboanga Medical School Foundation in the Philippines and the University Departments of Rural Health program in Australia, which provide rural clinical training opportunities for various health disciplines. 10. Investments in rural health education should focus on long-term sustainability and strengthening faculty in rural and remote areas. 11. Recruitment of rural-oriented faculty should be prioritized, and efforts should be made to allocate protected time for academic duties and ensure access to adequate information and communication technology infrastructure. 12. The economic and developmental impact of these institutions can yield high returns on investment, fostering multisectoral cooperation. 13. To maximize the effectiveness of rural health worker education facilities, alignment with policies on targeted student selection and locally relevant curricula is necessary. 14. Attention should also be given to the living, training, and studying conditions of students and faculty, ensuring they meet accepted local standards. 15. Integrating qualified rural health workers into training programs can complement policies on career development and enhance the profile of rural health workers. 16. Historically, health worker education has been concentrated in urban centers, often neglecting the specific skills required for resource-limited rural and remote settings. 17. Practical experiences in rural areas allow students to gain confidence and competence by working under guidance in rural health facilities, which can improve the quality of care and preparedness for practice. 18. Exposure to rural communities provides students with insights into primary health care delivery models and fosters self-efficacy in rural practice, which is strongly associated with intentions to remain in or return to rural practice. 19. The development of rural practice self-efficacy is vital for attracting, recruiting, and retaining health workers who are well-suited for rural and remote areas. 20. WHO recommends exposing students from various health disciplines to rural and remote communities and clinical practices to enhance their understanding and skills. 21. Harmonization and coordination between rural and urban education facilities are essential to ensure effective rural clinical experiences. 22. Rural health facilities used for teaching should allocate time for consultations, bedside rounds, procedures, and investigations, while also providing protected time for rural health staff to engage in teaching and professional development. 23. Policies should respect the rights and dignity of community members and health workers, with community engagement and stakeholder buy-in being crucial for successful implementation. 24. Student selection for rural experiences should prioritize those inclined toward rural practice and specialties to maximize recruitment impact. 25. Longer and multiple rural rotations can help students integrate into rural communities, gain interprofessional experience, and build trust within the community. 26. In contexts where language barriers exist, students should be given opportunities to learn the local language to enhance their effectiveness. 27. Training, support, and remuneration for instructors, supervisors, and teachers are necessary to ensure they can fulfill their roles effectively. 28. Curricula should include rural health topics and be periodically re-evaluated and revised to remain relevant to rural health needs. 29. Teachers with firsthand rural experience are ideal, but virtual learning tools can be employed where this is a challenge. 30. Education should equip students with competencies for rural practice, including clinical assessment and management in resource-limited settings, collaboration with other rural professionals, and understanding the culture and health-seeking behaviors of rural communities. 31. WHO strongly recommends aligning health worker education with rural health needs by including rural health topics in curricula and fostering social accountability. 32. Multisectoral collaboration and community engagement are essential for revising health worker education curricula to meet rural health needs. 33. Rural practice often involves a broader scope of practice due to limited access to other health workers and specialties, which should be considered in course content development. 34. Competency-based education should ensure that health workers are prepared to meet the health service needs of rural and remote populations. 35. Facilitating continuing education for rural and remote health workers is critical to maintaining their skills and ensuring high-quality care delivery.
